noteBlocks.lede: Your kidneys filter the blood and decide how much water goes back into it, which is what keeps the amount of water in your body steady. Everything else about water is fixed, so the volume of urine is the part that changes.

noteBlocks.text: The kidney, water balance and ADH

noteBlocks.md: Drink a litre of water and within an hour you need the toilet; sweat through a hot afternoon and you barely go at all. Your kidneys are filtering the blood and deciding how much water to keep.

noteBlocks.alt: The excretory system from the front: two bean-shaped kidneys either side of the body's two main blood vessels. Each kidney has a renal artery bringing blood from the main vessels and a renal vein taking it back. A ureter runs down from each kidney into the top of the bladder, and the urethra leads out of the bottom of the bladder.

noteBlocks.explain: The kidney. The bladder only stores the urine until it is released — Summer 2025 examiners reported bladder being given here.

noteBlocks.md:
**The names, in order.** Blood arrives through the **renal artery** and leaves through the **renal vein**. The **kidney** filters it and makes urine. Each kidney's urine runs down a **ureter** to the **bladder**, which stores it, and it leaves the body through the **urethra**.
**Ureter and urethra** are one letter apart and mean different things. The ureter carries urine **down** from the kidney; the urethra carries it **out**. Summer 2024's examiners were explicit that a spelling had to be near enough to be told apart from the other word.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?
options: the ureter
the urethra
the renal vein
noteBlocks.explain: The ureter. The urethra carries urine out of the body, and the renal vein carries blood, not urine.

noteBlocks.md: Cut a kidney in half and you see three regions the specification names: the **cortex** on the outside, the **medulla** inside it, and the **pelvis**, the space where urine collects before it enters the ureter. The outcome says in as many words that **no detail of the nephron is needed** — so glomerulus, Bowman's capsule and the loop of Henlé are not on this paper.

noteBlocks.md:
**Gained:** in **food**, in **drink**, and **made by respiration** — the water on the product side of the respiration equation is real water the body keeps.
**Lost:** by **evaporation of sweat**, by **evaporation during breathing** (which is why a cold window mists up), and as **urine** produced by the kidney.
Only the last of the six is under control. The kidney **filters the blood** and then **controls how much water is reabsorbed**, so the volume of urine is what changes when the balance shifts.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which is the third way the body gains water?
options: water made by respiration
water through the skin
water in the air
noteBlocks.explain: Respiration makes water as a product, and the body keeps it.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q8 and B1 Higher Q3
noteBlocks.md: Asked which organ produces urine, **quite a few candidates stated the bladder**. On the graph, some **read 120 instead of 110**, and others **read the wrong student's line**. Asked which student had lost the most water by other routes, quite a few named the right student but **fewer explained that they had produced the least urine**. And on the final part, **sweating** was given but **fewer also said breathing out**.

noteBlocks.title: Why urine volume is the only tap the body can turn
noteBlocks.md: Of the six routes water takes, five are fixed: you cannot decide how much your food holds, how much respiration makes, or how much evaporates. Only the kidney can be told to put water back.

noteBlocks.prompt: Besides sweating and urine, name the third way the body loses water.
noteBlocks.answer: breathing | breathing out | evaporation during breathing | exhalation
noteBlocks.explain: Evaporation during breathing. Summer 2025 examiners reported that candidates gave sweating but fewer also gave breathing out.

noteBlocks.md: **Reading a urine table.** If a student produced 20, 30, 40, 50 cm³ at the four check times, the **total** is 140 cm³ — add, do not average. The student who produces the **least** urine is the one who has lost the most water by the other two routes, and that comparison is what earns the explanation mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student produced 20, 30, 40, 50 cm³ of urine at the four check times. What was the total volume, in cm³?
noteBlocks.explain: 20 + 30 + 40 + 50 = 140 cm³. Add all four; the question asks for the total, not the mean.

noteBlocks.title: One sentence, learnt in one direction
noteBlocks.md: **ADH causes the kidney to reabsorb more water, so less urine is produced.** ADH is a hormone, so it is made by a gland, travels in the **blood** and acts on its target organ, the **kidney**. More ADH → more water reabsorbed → **less** urine, and the urine is more **concentrated**. Negative feedback is not required by the outcome, so you do not need the full loop — but you do need the direction.

The bottom row: too much water in the blood, less ADH released, the kidney reabsorbs less water, more urine that is more dilute.

noteBlocks.prompt: A person has been running in hot weather and has sweated a lot. What happens to their ADH?
options: More ADH is released, so less urine is produced
Less ADH is released, so more urine is produced
ADH is unchanged, because sweating is not the kidney's job
noteBlocks.answer: More ADH is released, so less urine is produced
noteBlocks.explain: Sweating removes water from the blood, so the body holds on to what is left: more ADH, more water reabsorbed, less urine.

noteBlocks.prompt: Someone drinks two litres of water quickly. What happens to the volume and concentration of their urine?
options: A larger volume of more dilute urine
A smaller volume of more concentrated urine
The same volume, but more concentrated
noteBlocks.answer: A larger volume of more dilute urine
noteBlocks.explain: Too much water in the blood means less ADH, so less water is reabsorbed: more urine, and more dilute.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niall is asked: 'A person sweats heavily and drinks nothing. Explain, in terms of ADH, what happens to the volume of urine they produce. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: Sweating removes water from the blood.
So a larger volume of urine is produced.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right, and the chain after line 2 is internally consistent — but it is running the wrong way. When the blood is short of water the body holds on to what it has: **more** ADH is released, the kidney reabsorbs **more** water, and a **smaller** volume of urine is produced.
correction: Sweating removes water from the blood.
So a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three: the first line earns its point, and the reasoning is neatly linked — which is why it is worth fixing the direction rather than relearning the whole chain. The sense check is the situation itself: someone who has sweated all afternoon and drunk nothing does not produce a lot of urine. Set the last box first — less water in, less urine out — and then fill in the two steps that get you there.
